The Parts You Use, and What Each One Does

You do not need the factory name of every gear to know which part is failing. Start with what the blind is doing wrong, then look at the part that does that job. Residential blinds share this layout even when the brand and the slat material change.

  • Headrail: The metal housing across the top. The lift and tilt parts sit inside it. If the blind hangs crooked, sags in the middle, or will not stay up, look here and at the brackets, not at a single slat.
  • Brackets: The clips that hold the headrail to the frame or the wall. A bracket that is too shallow lets the slats rub the trim. A bracket that pulls out of the wall drops one end of the blind.
  • Slats or vanes: The pieces that block the light. Tilting them opens a view. Lifting them stacks them out of the way. One bent slat is a slat problem. A whole blind that will not tilt is a control problem.
  • Tilt control: The wand, or the short cord, that turns the slats. Inside the headrail, a small gear turns a metal rod, and that rod rotates the slats together. When the slats slip back open, that gear is the usual part to replace. The gear is called the tilt mechanism.
  • Lift system: What holds the blind at a chosen height. On a corded blind, that is the cord and the cord lock that grips it. On a cordless blind, it is a spring inside the headrail that balances the weight. On a motorized blind, it is the motor. A blind that slowly drops has a lift problem.
  • Valance: The cover that hides the headrail. It does not lift or tilt anything. A cracked valance is a cover, not an operating failure.

How Edmonton Windows Change the Mount

The blind works when the headrail sits level and the slats can move without hitting the frame. Measure the opening before you choose a bracket. Hardware that fits a deep wood jamb can scrape a new vinyl window.

Frames you will see on local homes

  • Newer homes and renovations: Many vinyl windows have a shallow frame. A standard inside mount can stick past the opening or rub the glass and the crank. A slimmer headrail, or an outside mount on the trim or the wall, keeps the slats off the glass and lets the blind drop its full height.
  • Post-war bungalows and older double-hung windows: These are common in mature Edmonton neighborhoods. The wood jamb is often deep enough for an inside mount. Locks and crank handles still take space, so depth is a measurement, not an assumption.
  • Older plaster walls: A plastic anchor made for drywall often pulls out of plaster. One end of the blind then sags. The bracket needs a screw into a stud, or an anchor made for plaster.
  • Wide living-room glass: One long blind gets heavy in the middle. Two panels, or a center bracket, keep the headrail from bowing. You will see a small gap where the two bottom rails meet. That gap is the trade for a blind that stays level.
  • Bay, corner, and arch windows: Bay, bow, and corner windows need a headrail cut to each angle so neighboring slats do not hit each other. Arched windows usually keep a fixed piece in the curve and a working blind in the rectangle below. Large windows need the center bracket or the split headrail above.

What Local Weather Does to Parts, and What It Does Not

The wear we see on blinds in Edmonton homes comes from a long heating season, cold glass, sun on south and west windows, and steam in bathrooms and kitchens. None of these ruin every blind. They explain the repairs that come up most often.

  • Dry winter air: The furnace runs for months, so indoor air is dry. Dry air does not rust brackets. It can leave older cords and some plastic tilt gears feeling stiffer. If slats on a sunny window will not hold an angle after years of use, check the tilt gear first. That is a common repair. It is not a date you can put on a calendar.
  • Sun on south and west glass: Afternoon sun fades color and, over years, can make some plastic parts brittle. A fade-resistant finish slows the color change. It does not stop a cord, a spring, or a gear from wearing out with daily use. Ask about the finish on the windows that take the sun, and expect ordinary mechanical wear on every window.
  • Condensation on cold glass: On older windows, winter glass gets cold enough to sweat. Water that sits on a steel bracket or a wood slat is what leads to rust and swelling. Newer sealed windows do this less often. If the sill is wet most mornings, keep the blind off the glass and skip unfinished wood in that opening.
  • Bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms: The moisture is steam from showers, cooking, and laundry. Real wood can cup if it stays damp. Faux wood and aluminum blinds are preferred in damp areas as they do not absorb moisture like wood. They do not dry the room out. Use the fan, wipe standing water, and the slats are less likely to twist. Leave cleaner sitting on a coated slat and the finish can still mark.

Manual and Motorized Controls, Including What a Motor Does Not Fix

The repairs we see most often are lift parts and tilt parts, because those are the pieces people use every day. The control you pick changes which parts you touch, and which parts sit inside the headrail instead.

A common local case is a living room in a newer house, with tall windows behind a sofa. You cannot reach the top without climbing. A cord or a wand is fine when someone can reach it safely. A motor is worth discussing when those windows are raised every day, or when several windows should move together.

What each control wears

  • Tilt wand: You turn the slats without a cord hanging in the room. The wand can crack, and the hook under the headrail is usually a small piece you can swap. If the hook inside the headrail breaks, the blind comes off the brackets.
  • Cord lift: You pull a cord, and a cord lock grips it. Those two parts take the wear, especially if the cord is pulled to the side. This is the system most likely to fray or slip.
  • Cordless lift: A spring inside the headrail balances the weight. You move the bottom rail and it should stay put. The spring is still a mechanical part. If one side drops, it needs adjustment or a new spring. Cordless removes the hanging cord. It does not remove wear.
  • Motor: A motor in the headrail raises and lowers the blind. On many blinds it tilts the slats too. You use a remote, a phone, or a short wand that only tells the motor to run. You stop yanking the lift cord, so the cord lock is spared that abuse. The motor, its gears, and the battery do the work instead. Those parts can fail while the slats still look new. Fewer cord repairs are a fair expectation. A longer life for the whole blind is not a promise the motor can make.

PowerView® Automation is the grouped version. A remote, the app, or a schedule moves several blinds together, which helps on a bank of tall windows. Motorized Blinds & Shades - Hunter Douglas. Each blind still has its own motor, and its own battery or power supply, to look after.

Motorized Hunter Douglas® blinds are a reach and a cord-safety choice as much as a wear choice. The operating cord stays in the headrail, which matters with children or pets. A cordless blind does that without a motor. Choose the motor when you also want the blind to move without a pull, and plan on charging or replacing the battery as normal upkeep.

Pairing Parts With the Room

A blind holds up in ordinary use when the material fits the room and the headrail fits the frame. That means the slats stay usable and the control keeps working with normal service. It does not mean a set number of years, and it does not mean the blind is maintenance-free.

  • Sunny windows: On south and west glass, a fade-resistant finish slows color change, and the lift has to be rated for the size and weight of that blind. The finish does not stop the cord, the spring, or the motor from wearing with use.
  • Damp rooms: An aluminum headrail with faux wood or aluminum slats is the usual pairing, because those slats do not absorb steam the way wood does. They are less likely to twist if you vent the room. They are not mold-proof, and they are not a stand-in for a fan or for a window that closes.
  • Inside mount: The headrail and the bottom rail need a small gap at each side so they do not grind the jamb every time you lift the blind. If the frame is too shallow for that gap, mount on the trim or the wall.
  • Plaster: Fasten into a stud, or use a plaster anchor. A failed anchor shows up as a blind that leans, not as a broken slat.

Ordering a Replacement Part That Fits

A part that looks right can still be the wrong size. Headrail shapes, tilt gears, and cord thickness change between brands, and between years of the same brand. Matching by eye is how a replacement jams.

What to record before you order

  • The label: Look inside the headrail or on the bottom rail. The sticker names the maker and often the date. That sticker matters more than the color of the slat.
  • The size and the control: Note the slat width, the shape of the headrail, and whether you tilt with a wand, a cord, or a motor. A photo of the broken part next to the label is enough to confirm the match. You do not need special measuring tools for the first call.
  • Taking it down: The blind removal tips show how to release the brackets without bending the headrail or pulling the anchor out of the wall.

Where the part has to come from

Hardware stores stock generic wands and brackets. They do not stock the tilt gears and end pieces for most Hunter Douglas® and ALTA® Window Fashions blinds. FAQ

Short answers to the repair questions we hear most often about the parts of a blind and the system that moves them.

QuestionAnswer
Which parts fail most often?Tilt gears and cord locks, because they are used every day. On south and west windows, some plastic tilt gears also get brittle after years of sun and dry winter air. If the slats will not hold an angle, or the blind will not stay up, check those parts. Plenty of blinds never need that repair.
How does a cordless blind stay at a height?A spring inside the headrail balances the weight of the slats and the bottom rail. You move the bottom rail and the spring holds it there. If one side sinks, the spring needs adjustment or replacement. The spring wears, the same way a cord lock wears on an older blind.
Can you replace a tilt wand without taking the blind down?Usually, yes. The wand clips to a hook just under the headrail. Unclip the broken wand and clip a new one on. If the hook itself snapped off inside the headrail, the blind has to come off the brackets so the tilt gear can be reached.
Does a motor make a blind last longer?It can cut wear on the cord and the cord lock, because you are no longer pulling them. It does not remove friction from the blind. The motor and its gears do that work instead, and the battery needs charging or replacement. Use motorization to reach tall windows and to keep cords out of the room. Any extra years of service are a possible result of gentler daily use, not a result you can count on.
Should a warped faux wood slat be replaced on its own?One slat can be replaced when a matching piece is still available. If many slats have bent, a new blind usually costs less than rebuilding the ladder strings. Faux wood handles bathroom steam better than real wood. Heat, a tight fit against the frame, or a slat left against wet glass can still bend it.
